doc.title: Orrin Keepnews interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 7, 2002

title: No rehearsals, working rhythm sections and the Really Big session
summary: He says Riverside dates used musicians who knew each other, citing Jimmy Heath's Really Big and Monk with Hawkins and Coltrane.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: companies. That could not happen today even though people are constantly still trying to do it. And there were a number of other factors you see. We were kind of famous for not having rehearsals. Even though there was written material but what you have to point out then is we were working and made sure we were working with people who were tremendously familiar with playing with each other. If I had a rhythm section that technically didn’t have a rehearsal they nevertheless had been playing together probably for about ten years, that’ll do as far as being able to get things out of each other and being able to work together. And that would be not that easy to do today, though there is still a tendency, I mean I fight hard to get — to work with people who know each other who can shortcut the time and don’t have to be introduced to each other at the date, but you just won’t get back to — that was the climate. I mean the scene in New York was a very real part of what we did, a lot of interaction between a lot of talented musicians. And again at Riverside there was a tremendous amount of people associated with the label playing on other people’s dates, not because we asked them to because they told us — I’m going to be — I mean the second record I did with Jimmy Heath, who everybody really loved, was because Jimmy was such a great writer we just pulled it together and got Jimmy, we did like a ten-piece date, seven horns kind of thing. And it was easy, we knew who the bass player and the drummer were going to be, they were going to be Percy and Tootie [Heath], but there were two trumpets on that album called “Really Big,” which is a wonderful, medium band, Jimmy Heath album from about 1961. Well the trumpet players on that are Nat Adderley and Clark Terry because they told me they were going to be. The alto is Cannonball because he said so. And Cannonball only plays one solo on the thing. We were not trying to milk the famous artist and have this really, like it was featuring him or something. But there he was because he damn well said he was going to be there. And I think for some reason we changed piano players between sessions so we had I think Flanagan on one and Cedar Walton on the other, that kind of thing. Now some of that is like names didn’t have the same meaning that they do today. I mean everybody says wow, a Thelonious Monk record with John Coltrane and Coleman Hawkins on it. Wow. Well it’s a wonderful record but it was not a record that was made with two famous tenor players. It was a record made with one tenor player who was considered to be over the hill, and one who hadn’t happened yet. But those are important points to remember when you’re milking the nostalgia of an old cat like me to remember that a lot of times you have to look below the surface. It’s the same as don’t take Miles Davis’ word for anything. Investigate what the truth of it is. It’s the same kind of situation. Don’t just look at the personnel listing and say wow, those guys must have spent a lot of money to put this band together.
